patchAnchors.fullText: Appendix B: Faiths and Cosmologies of Aethel
patchAnchors.observedPhrase: Appendix B: Faiths and Cosmologies of Aethel

patchAnchors.fullText: The beliefs recorded in this appendix are mortal theology, not objective cosmic history. Priests, scholars, and cults across Aethel have spent millennia reasoning about forces they cannot fully perceive. What follows is what the faithful believe: a creation myth, a pantheon of worshiped faces, and a diagram of the planes — sincerely held, widely taught, and useful for understanding how ordinary people in Aethel think about the divine. Your character may treat this as literal truth. Deeper mysteries of the Spiral and the Crucible may surface only through play; even then, the wider world does not rewrite its temples overnight. Scholars may also speak of the First Choir — seven named virtues (Korvelan, Vaerilune, Delvaran, Shaelara, Xalarex, Thalirion, and Virellian) — as part of the wider Spiral story. That knowledge is not secret, but it is not tavern talk either.
patchAnchors.observedPhrase: mortal theology, not objective cosmic history

patchAnchors.fullText: In the beginning, mortal theologians say, there was only the Void — a vast, formless expanse of potential. Within this nothingness they name two primordial principles: Lumina, the Radiant Consciousness, and Umbra, the Abyssal Depth. Neither light nor dark, neither good nor evil, these twin abstractions of creation are how priests reason about first causes — not laboratory descriptions of beings scholars can point to in the sky. In the folk story, for eons beyond counting Lumina and Umbra drifted through the Void, unaware of their own existence. Then, in a moment that transcends time itself, they became conscious. Lumina's first thought was of wonder; Umbra's was of curiosity. As their awareness grew, so did their desire to understand the nature of their own being.

As the planes stabilized following the Sundering, folk religion teaches that fragments of Lumina and Umbra's consciousness crystallized into the first gods. These divine faces — worship masks mortals place on real cosmic forces they cannot otherwise name — embody specific aspects of those primordial principles, each representing a particular facet of existence as temples understand it.
patchAnchors.observedPhrase: worship masks mortals place on real cosmic forces

patchAnchors.fullText: These fifteen Greater Gods, known collectively as the Fifteenfold Pantheon (or Primeval Pantheon in older temple texts), shape how mortals name the fundamental nature of the cosmos. Later, as civilizations arose, Lesser Gods and cultural pantheons emerged from belief and need — the most local tier of this worship hierarchy. Most ordinary people treat the Fifteenfold as literally true; this appendix records that faith.

Mortal cosmographers diagram the planes as a concentric wheel, with the Material Plane at its center and other planes arranged around it in concentric rings. This Wheel of Testimony is a teaching tool for organizing planar reports and temple doctrine — not a claim that explorers have surveyed the complete architecture of existence. Some planes overlap with the Material Plane in places, creating regions where their influence is stronger and their denizens might cross over more easily.
patchAnchors.observedPhrase: This Wheel of Testimony is a teaching tool

patchAnchors.fullText: Temple historians call the War of Chains and Teeth the oldest open war among the Lower Planes: the ordered legions of Asmodeus's Nine Infernal Courts against the demonic hordes of the Abyss. In the folk telling, the conflict sharpened after the Sundering and the forging of the Divine Pact, when Asmodeus's realm of contracts and hierarchy and the Abyss's hunger for unbound ruin could no longer share a quiet border. Every escalation strains the Divine Pact that keeps Heaven and Hell from replacing mortal choice with open divine war — priests disagree whether the War of Chains and Teeth protects the Pact by exhausting the fiends or endangers it by feeding the very dissonance the Pact was meant to manage.
